summary: RFC 2026 describes how the IESG reviews Proposed Standards and characterizes their maturity. This document updates RFC 2026 with a more current and accurate characterization of what a Proposed Standard is.

plainLanguage.summary: This Best Current Practice updates how RFC 2026 describes Proposed Standards. It explains the review and maturity expected, while leaving other standards-process procedures unchanged.

questions: how mature is a proposed standard rfc
what is the difference between proposed standard and internet standard
what review does a proposed standard receive
when can the iesg require implementation experience
subtitle: Updates the IETF's description of the maturity and review of Proposed Standards.

tldr.problem: The description of Proposed Standards in RFC 2026 no longer accurately reflected the IETF's evolved review process.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7127 replaces that characterization with one describing stability, resolved design choices, significant review and community interest.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 2026 and says known limitations in a Proposed Standard must be communicated clearly.

today: RFC 7127 is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 2026. The unit metadata does not list it as obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why the Characterization Changed
sections.content:
In the two decades after RFC 2026 was published, the IETF changed how it reviews Proposed Standard RFCs. RFC 7127 says Section 4.1.1 of RFC 2026 no longer described Proposed Standards accurately.

This document updates that characterization only. It does not change the maintenance procedures in RFC 2026 or RFC 6410; those documents should be read with it for the full standards process.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF's review process changed over time. This RFC updates one description and leaves the other procedures in the referenced documents.

sections.title: Review of Proposed Standards
sections.content:
Proposed Standard is the entry-level maturity for the Standards Track, and a specific IESG action is required to place a specification there. The RFC says that progression through the former sequence of Proposed Standard, Draft Standard and Internet Standard is rare.

It notes that many Proposed Standards are deployed and used as stable protocols. They have generally had open development, community review and formal cross-discipline reviews, including security review; implementations and interoperable code may add experience.
sections.plainLanguage: Proposed Standard is the entry level of the Standards Track. Such documents have undergone open development and significant review.

sections.title: What a Proposed Standard Means
sections.content:
A Proposed Standard is stable, has resolved known design choices, received significant community review and appears to have enough community interest to be valuable. Implementation or operational experience is usually not required, though the RFC calls it highly desirable.

The IESG may require such experience for specifications that materially affect core Internet protocols or may have significant operational impact. A Proposed Standard should have no known technical omissions and can be deployed, but it may be revised if problems or better solutions emerge.
sections.plainLanguage: A Proposed Standard is stable, reviewed and considered useful. The IESG can still require experience before approving some specifications.

references.text: Bradner, S., "The Internet Standards Process -- Revision 3", BCP 9, RFC 2026, October 1996.
Housley, R., Crocker, D., and E. Burger, "Reducing the Standards Track to Two Maturity Levels", BCP 9, RFC 6410, October 2011.
